An interactive field guide · 96 terms, 7 categories

The Language of the Camera

Every shot, angle, movement, perspective, composition technique, advanced term and special effect in cinematography — each on its own card, and each category taught hands-on in its own lab. Search for a term, filter by category, and expand any card for its effect, best use, pitfalls and a film to watch it in.

A camera on dolly tracks — the machine whose position and movement this guide teaches you to read.

How the cards work

Every card follows the same pattern: Definition — Effect / purpose — When to use — Watch out — Example. Shot size answers how much of the subject is in frame; angle answers from where, and tilted how; movement answers how the camera travels or pivots; composition answers where things sit inside the frame.

A note on confidence

Core definitions are standard textbook usage and agree across multiple independent sources (listed at the end). Film examples are well-known, illustrative examples — a film cited for one technique almost always uses many others. Crop points for shot sizes are conventions, not millimetre rules; sources vary slightly, and that is flagged where it matters.

The core grammar

A shot is an uninterrupted run of frames. Meaning is rarely made by one choice alone — it is made by size + angle + movement + lens + light + edit together. A useful rule of thumb from the sources: the size of a subject in frame should be proportional to its importance at that moment — go closer to raise emotional stakes, go wider to raise context, scale or distance.

Category 01 · Framing scale

Shot Sizes

Field size is set by camera–subject distance and focal length. The scale runs widest → tightest. Sources agree on the crop points, with small variations — a medium close-up is chest-up in some guides, waist-up in others — so treat crop points as conventions, not measurements. Try the scale yourself first:

Framing lab

One figure, nine framings

The same actor in the same landscape, reframed from extreme wide to extreme close-up. Notice how the story changes as the world falls away and the face takes over.

Extreme Wide Shot

Framing
When to use
Watch it in

Diagram is a schematic: real crop points vary by production and by the convention notes above.

Extreme Wide Shot EWS / ELS

Shot size

The subject is tiny against the landscape, often barely visible; the world is the subject.

Effect / purposeGrandeur, scale, isolation, insignificance; orients the viewer in a world.

When to useOpenings, epic landscapes, a lone figure in a desert or city.

ExampleLawrence of Arabia (1962) desert vistas; The Lord of the Rings landscapes.

Wide Shot WS / LS

Shot size

The whole subject plus substantial surroundings — context and action in the same frame.

Effect / purposeNarrative distance and geography: the audience understands where everyone is and how the space works.

When to useEstablishing a location, choreography, a character entering a world.

ExampleThe opening of a Western town; dance or fight choreography shown in full.

Full Shot FS

Shot size

Head to toe: the subject fills the frame, but the surroundings are still visible.

Effect / purposeBody language, costume, movement and setting read at once.

When to useA character's entrance, a performance, a confrontation where posture matters.

ExampleA hero walking into frame in full costume.

Medium Long Shot MLS / MWS

Shot size

Knees or thighs up — also called the medium wide shot.

Effect / purposeBalances expression, gesture and background; a workhorse for action-dialogue.

When to useScenes where hands, props and movement matter as well as the face.

ExampleA character drawing a weapon, cooking, or working at a desk.

Cowboy / American Shot CS

Shot size

Mid-thigh up. Named for Westerns: it frames the gun and holster at the hip while keeping the face readable.

Effect / purposeA stylish, grounded dialogue framing where stance and a waist-worn object carry story.

When to useWesterns; any scene where a waist-worn object or stance is story-critical.

ExampleClassic John Ford and Sergio Leone gunfighter framings.

Medium Shot MS

Shot size

Waist up — the default dialogue shot: face plus upper-body gesture, with some environment.

Effect / purposeNeutral, conversational coverage; the audience reads expression and gesture together.

When to useConversations, interviews, two-person dialogue coverage.

ExampleMost TV and film dialogue.

Medium Close-Up MCU

Shot size

Chest or mid-chest up. The face dominates and the environment recedes.

Effect / purposeIntimacy without the intensity of a full close-up.

When to useEmotional dialogue, reactions, a character realising something.

ExampleA confession, or a quiet reaction in drama.

Close-Up CU

Shot size

The face — or a significant object — fills the frame.

Effect / purposeIntimacy, emotion, detail. It forces the audience to notice what the character feels, or what matters.

When to useReveals, reactions, a crucial object, a lie told with the eyes.

ExampleA tear, a trembling hand, a decision registering silently.

Extreme Close-Up ECU

Shot size

Part of a face — eyes, lips — or a tiny detail fills the frame. Also called a detail shot.

Effect / purposeMaximum intensity: obsession, clue, dread. At this scale the subject becomes abstract.

When to useA trigger finger, an eye, a key turning, a clue the audience must not miss.

ExampleLeone's eye close-ups in The Good, the Bad and the Ugly; a ticking bomb detail.

Two-Shot

Relational

Two subjects in one frame, usually at medium or medium-wide scale. Not a size — a job: it stages a relationship.

Effect / purposeShows relationship, distance and power between two people in space — who is closer, taller, turned away?

When to useDialogue, romance, rivalry — held in a single frame rather than cut into singles.

Watch outIf one actor dominates the frame unintentionally, the relationship reads as unequal.

Over-the-Shoulder OTS

Relational

Camera behind one subject's shoulder and the back of their head, looking at the other subject.

Effect / purposeConnection and point of view at once: the foreground shoulder anchors us with the listener. It is also an angle (§Angles) — it places the audience with one character.

When to useDialogue, alternating with its reverse — see Shot-Reverse-Shot in Advanced Terms.

Watch outKeep the foreground shoulder soft, out of focus and small enough not to swallow the frame; keep eyelines consistent.

Insert (Cut-In)

Relational

A close shot of a detail within the ongoing action — a letter, a photo, hands, a weapon — cut in to clarify or emphasise.

Effect / purpose"Look at this, it matters." The insert points the audience's attention at a plot-critical detail.

When to useClues, plot objects, a character's hands doing something telling.

ExampleThe close-up of a letter or a key in a thriller.

Cutaway

Relational

A shot away from the main action — a reaction, a clock, a crowd, an object elsewhere — then back to the main action.

Effect / purposeContext, reaction, time passing, or a breather; it also lets an editor hide a cut.

When to useCutting to a listener's or audience's reaction during a speech.

Watch outA cutaway with no story link feels like a mistake.

Establishing Shot

Relational

Usually a wide or extreme-wide shot at the start of a scene (or film) that tells the audience where, when and in what kind of world we are.

Effect / purposeOrientation, mood and scale, delivered before the story starts moving.

When to useEvery new location, time change, or return after an absence.

ExampleA city skyline opening a sequence; a desert town before we meet its people.

Master Shot

Relational

A shot that covers a whole scene from one vantage point, start to finish, with all major players in view — often wide, but it can move, and can be medium or even close if it still covers the action.

Effect / purposeThe spatial safety net: the editor can always return to it.

When to useShoot it first in the "master scene" method, then shoot coverage (OTS, close-ups) to cut into it.

Watch outA master that is too wide for too long feels flat — it is a foundation, not necessarily the final rhythm. A long dinner-table scene played in one wide take is the classic case.

Common mistakes — shot sizes: jumping straight from wide to extreme close-up with no intermediate size (disorienting); cutting between near-identical sizes (see the 30-degree rule in Advanced Terms); using a close-up for information the audience needs in wide, such as the geography of a fight; using a wide shot for an emotion only a face can carry.
Category 02 · From where, tilted how

Camera Angles

An angle is the camera's vertical relationship to the subject, plus its tilt. It is not the same as shot size — a close-up can be low-angle and a wide shot high-angle — and not the same as camera height alone (see "Camera Height vs Angle" in Advanced Terms). Angle is where power enters the frame: look up at someone and they grow; look down and they shrink.

Angle lab · Where do you put the camera?

Move the camera, change the power

Left: the set from the side — the camera (gold) moves, the actor (centre) never does. Right: what the audience actually sees. Same actor, same distance, same shot size — only the camera's height and tilt change.

On set — side view

On screen — the audience's frame

Eye-Level

Camera placement
When to use
Watch out

Eye-Level

Angle

Camera at the subject's eye height, held level.

Effect / purposeNeutral, natural, equal. The audience meets the character as a peer; realism and identification.

When to useDefault dialogue, documentary, romance — when you want no power commentary.

ExampleMost dialogue in Casablanca and Before Sunrise.

Low Angle

Angle

Camera below the subject, tilted up — classically around 45°.

Effect / purposeThe subject looks larger, powerful, dominant, heroic or threatening; the background compresses to sky.

When to useHeroes, villains, authority, awe; a child looking up at an adult.

Watch outIt can accidentally make a sympathetic character look menacing.

ExampleSuperhero entrances; Citizen Kane's low angles on Kane.

High Angle

Angle

Camera above the subject, tilted down.

Effect / purposeThe subject looks smaller, weaker, vulnerable, trapped or observed; more of the surroundings show.

When to usePowerlessness, isolation, surveillance, a character overwhelmed.

Watch outIt can make a powerful character look comic.

ExampleA character lost in a crowd, seen from above.

Bird's-Eye / Top-Down

Angle

Camera directly overhead, looking straight down at ~90°.

Effect / purposeOmniscient, detached, god-like. Patterns, layouts, choreography and geography become visible; people become pieces on a board.

When to useEstablishing a location, dance or battle formations, a maze, a crime-scene layout.

ExampleBusby Berkeley overhead dance numbers; overhead shots in The Shining and the Parasite stairwell.

Worm's-Eye

Angle

Camera at ground level, tilted straight up at ~90° — the extreme low angle.

Effect / purposeThe subject towers, gigantic and forbidding; disorientation and awe.

When to useSkyscrapers, monsters, trees, a figure looming over a fallen character.

ExampleA monster or a building looming over the camera.

Dutch / Canted Angle

Angle

The camera is rolled sideways so the horizon runs diagonally. Also called an oblique angle.

Effect / purposeUnease, imbalance, tension, psychological distress — a world "off-kilter".

When to useThriller, horror, madness, intoxication, a character losing control.

Watch outOn every shot it stops meaning "unease" and starts meaning "sloppy"; tilt so slightly it reads as an accident and it fails — tilt enough to look intentional.

ExampleThe Third Man (1949) and its tilted Vienna.

Shoulder-Level

Angle

Camera at the standing subject's shoulder height, held level — the classic OTS height.

Effect / purposeNatural conversational height; slightly more intimate than eye level in a crowd.

When to useDialogue, walk-and-talks, OTS coverage.

ExampleStandard over-the-shoulder dialogue.

Hip-Level

Angle

Camera at hip height.

Effect / purposeGrounded, slightly low, dynamic. Emphasises stride, stance, and weapons or tools at the waist; a "following from behind" documentary feel.

When to useWalking shots, Westerns, action following a character.

ExampleA gunfighter's walk; a character striding through a crowd.

Knee-Level

Angle

Camera at knee height, looking slightly up.

Effect / purposeMore dramatic than hip-level: legs and scale dominate, the background rises. Child-height or "small creature" perspective.

When to useChildren, animals, low action, a character rising or falling.

ExampleA child's POV world; a hero rising from the ground.

Point-of-View POV

Angle

The camera sits where a character's eyes would be; the audience sees exactly (or approximately) what the character sees.

Effect / purposeImmersion, identification, suspense — we know only what they know — and sometimes disorientation.

When to useHorror (the killer's POV), a character discovering something, first-person sequences.

ExampleHalloween (1978), the opening killer POV; Rear Window (1954), Jeff's POV through binoculars and camera; Lady in the Lake (1947) and Hardcore Henry (2015) as feature-length POV experiments.

Subjective Camera

Angle

The camera embodies a character's experience — POV shots, but also shots coloured by a character's emotion: shaky when panicked, distorted or dreamlike when drugged, a rack focus to what they notice.

Effect / purposeThe audience is inside a mind, not just a pair of eyes.

Watch outA POV shot is not automatically subjective: a purely optical POV — just what the eyes see, with no emotional colouring — sits between subjective and objective.

Objective Camera

Angle

The camera is an impartial, detached observer — a "fly on the wall" that records events and lets the audience judge.

Effect / purposeFairness and detachment. Long and wide shots, static observational framing and deadpan coverage favour objectivity. In comedy, the detachment can make absurdity funnier and colder, because the camera refuses to tell you when to laugh.

Directing tipUse the contrast deliberately: establish objectively, then go subjective at the emotional peak — or subjective panic, then a cold objective wide that shows how small the panic is in the world.

Category 03 · How the camera travels

Camera Movements

The governing rule: move for a reason — to reveal, to follow, to intensify, or to change a relationship. The moves below are grouped by what physically happens: pivoting in place, travelling through space, changing the lens, or changing focus.

Movement lab · How does the camera travel?

Watch the path, then watch the frame

Top: the set from above — the gold camera, its view cone, and the actor. Press Play the move and follow the gold dot: does the camera pivot in place, travel through space, circle, or stay put while only the lens changes? Bottom right: what that path does to the picture. Try Dolly In, then Zoom In — the actor ends the same size, but only the dolly moves you through space.

Animation loops while playing. The frame preview (in the readout) shows the picture changing.

Static / Locked-Off

Frame preview — schematic. Watch the actor's size, the background object's size, and whether the two change together (zoom) or at different rates (dolly — that difference is parallax).

How the camera moves
Rig / placement
When to use

Static / Locked-Off

Movement

The camera does not move at all — tripod, locked head.

Effect / purposeStability, objectivity, tension — the frame becomes a stage — and deadpan comedy. Performance and blocking carry the scene.

When to useDialogue, surveillance, horror (waiting), formal or comic detachment.

ExampleLocked-off dinner-table scenes in The Royal Tenenbaums; security-camera horror.

Pan

Movement

The camera pivots left or right on a fixed base.

Effect / purposeReveals, follows a lateral subject, and connects two people or places in one shot without a cut.

When to useFollowing a walker, sweeping a room, connecting speaker to listener.

ExampleWes Anderson's lateral pans in The Grand Budapest Hotel.

Tilt

Movement

The camera pivots up or down on a fixed base.

Effect / purposeReveals scale and height; connects feet to face or ground to sky; creates surprise.

When to useA tall building, a character's full stature, a reveal from feet upward.

ExampleA tilt up a skyscraper; a tilt down to a body on the ground.

Pan-Tilt

Movement

A combined pivot on both axes, usually on a tripod head or gimbal.

Effect / purposeFollows diagonal or unpredictable movement; a "looking around" feel.

When to useSport; a character moving through a room diagonally — crossing and climbing stairs in one move.

Dolly / Tracking / Trucking

Movement

The camera physically travels — on rails, wheels, a vehicle or a Steadicam. Dolly = in or out; tracking = following a subject; trucking (or crab) = sideways.

Effect / purposeImmersion and momentum, with parallax — foreground and background move at different speeds, so space feels real. Intimacy when pushing in.

When to useFollowing a character, entering a world, a slow push-in on a realisation.

ExampleThe Goodfellas Copacabana entrance; the Shining tricycle tracking shots; the long tracking shots of Children of Men.

Push-In (Dolly In)

Movement

The camera moves toward the subject during the shot.

Effect / purposeGrowing intimacy, tension and focus; a character's inner shift. The world narrows to them.

When to useA realisation, a decision, a threat approaching.

ExampleA slow push-in on a face as bad news lands.

Pull-Out / Pull-Back

Movement

The camera moves away from the subject during the shot.

Effect / purposeContext returns and isolation grows; the character shrinks into their world. Endings and reveals.

When to useThe end of a scene, a character left alone, a twist that reframes everything.

ExampleA pull-back at the end of a scene revealing the character was not alone.

Crane / Jib

Movement

The camera rides a long arm — lifted high, lowered, or swung over a set.

Effect / purposeGrandeur and god-like reveals; smooth vertical and lateral arcs impossible on foot. Openings and finales.

When to useEstablishing a world, a crowd, a ceremony; a crane-up to end a film.

ExampleThe opening crane shot of Touch of Evil (1958); crane finales over a landscape.

Steadicam / Gimbal

Movement

An operator-worn stabiliser (Steadicam) or motorised gimbal gives smooth, free handheld movement.

Effect / purposeFluid, floating, dreamlike or immersive travel through real spaces — stairs, crowds, corridors.

When to useLong takes; following a character through a building; POV-like flow without shake.

Watch outA move so smooth it feels weightless can undercut a gritty scene.

ExampleGoodfellas' Copacabana shot; Birdman (2014), edited to feel like one continuous flow.

Handheld / Shaky Cam

Movement

The camera is held by hand, unstabilised; its shake stays in the image.

Effect / purposeUrgency, realism, instability, documentary immediacy, panic.

When to useChases, war, documentary, a character's breakdown.

Watch outShake that makes the audience seasick rather than tense; overusing it when the scene needs calm.

ExampleSaving Private Ryan's battle chaos; The Blair Witch Project; the Bourne films' action.

Drone / Aerial

Movement

The camera flies on a drone — historically, a helicopter.

Effect / purposeSweeping scale, geography, pursuit from the air, impossible angles.

When to useLandscapes, chases, establishing a remote location, a reveal from above.

ExampleAerial establishing shots in modern epics; FPV drone dives in action sequences.

Zoom (In / Out)

Movement

The focal length changes; the camera does not move. The image magnifies or shrinks from a fixed position.

Effect / purposeFeels observational or voyeuristic — like binoculars — or, in fast zooms, startling. A period style in 1970s cinema.

When to useSpying and observational scenes, a sudden detail, a retro or documentary feel.

Watch outOverused zoom reads as observation or a period effect when a dolly would immerse; don't let a zoom fight a dolly — use one.

ExampleThe slow zooms of Barry Lyndon; snap zooms in The Office and horror.

Whip Pan

Movement

An extremely fast pan, fast enough to blur the image into streaks.

Effect / purposeEnergy, surprise, a comic or frantic transition; links two spaces in a blur.

When to useComedy, action transitions, a character's head snapping toward a sound.

Watch outSo fast, so often, that the audience loses the geography of the scene.

ExampleEdgar Wright and Sam Raimi films; Wes Anderson's fast pans as punctuation.

Arc Shot / Orbit

Movement

The camera moves in a partial circle (arc) or a full circle (orbit, 360°) around the subject.

Effect / purposeA changing perspective on a static moment: rising tension, a character surrounded, a hero moment. A fast 360° orbit isolates the subject as the stable centre of chaos.

When to useConfrontations, realisations, reveals — "the world turns around them" moments.

ExampleThe Matrix (1999) bullet-time orbit, in its extreme form; slow arcs around a couple in romance and drama.

Pedestal

Movement

The whole camera moves straight up or down — like an elevator — without pivoting (contrast with a tilt).

Effect / purposeA clean vertical reveal; a change in status — rise reads as power, fall as vulnerability.

When to useFollowing someone sitting, standing or climbing; a reveal from below a table; a vertical set.

ExampleA pedestal up to a speaker on a stage; a pedestal down as a character collapses or sits.

Roll

Movement

The camera rotates around its own lens axis — the Dutch angle in motion.

Effect / purposeDisorientation, dizziness, a world spinning; a barrel-roll stunt feel.

When to useVertigo, a fall, a dream, an action spin.

ExampleBarrel-roll and vortex shots; Inception-style disorientation.

Follow Shot

Movement

The camera travels with a moving subject, keeping a constant relationship — in front, behind, or beside.

Effect / purposeJourney, pursuit, companionship: the audience travels with the character.

When to useWalk-and-talks, chases, entrances, a character leading us into a new place.

ExampleA character walking through a market with the camera beside or behind them.

Reveal (as a move)

Movement

Any move — dolly, pan, tilt, crane, pedestal, rack focus, a foreground wipe — that withholds the key information, then shows it.

Effect / purposeSurprise, suspense, reframing: the meaning of the shot changes in its last second.

When to usePlot twists, a character who was hidden, a location's true scale.

ExampleThe camera pans past a foreground pillar to reveal a crowd; a crane rises over a wall to reveal an army.

Rack Focus / Focus Pull

Movement

Focus shifts from one depth plane to another within the same shot, the camera largely still. Technically a lens move — used as camera language.

Effect / purposeRedirects attention without a cut; shows a relationship between foreground and background; a power shift — who is sharp is who matters now.

When to useA character in the background becomes important; a foreground object reveals a background reaction.

ExampleForeground coffee cup → background couple; a villain sharpening into focus behind a hero.

Zoom vs dolly — the key distinction

Dolly moves the camera through space: parallax changes, perspective shifts, and you feel you are walking into the scene. Zoom changes the lens: everything magnifies together, there is no parallax, and you feel you are looking closer from where you stand. Choose dolly for immersion and intimacy; zoom for observation, detachment or stylised emphasis. Mix them in opposite directions and you get the dolly zoom — see Special Effects.

Common mistakes — movement: moving because the gear is available, not because the story needs it; a zoom that fights a dolly (use one); whip pans so fast the audience loses geography; a Steadicam move so smooth it feels weightless in a gritty scene — in animation and CG, deliberately add weight and inertia (see the Director's Guide).
Category 04 · Whose knowledge do we share?

Perspectives & Viewpoints

These are narrative positions, not just camera positions. The same shot size and angle can serve different perspectives depending on whose knowledge the audience shares. Subjective means filtered through a character — their eyes, fear, memory; objective means unfiltered observation, the camera as witness. Most films alternate: objective for geography and fairness, subjective for peaks of feeling.

Perspective lab · Whose eyes, whose knowledge?

One scene, six viewpoints

The scene never changes: a hero talks with a friend, and a threat waits hidden behind the door — the hero cannot see it. Only the viewpoint changes. Watch two things: what the frame shows, and the gap between what the hero knows and what you know. That gap is where suspense lives.

What the hero knows

What you (the audience) know

Third-Person Limited

Where the camera sits
The knowledge gap
Watch it in

First-Person

Perspective

We see as the character: POV shots and subjective camera, sometimes the character's hands or body in frame. Knowledge = only what that character knows.

Effect / purposeMaximum immersion and identification — and maximum limitation: we cannot see the character's face reacting.

Watch outA whole film in first person can lose emotional connection, because we never see the hero react — a criticism made of Lady in the Lake.

ExampleLady in the Lake (1947), Hardcore Henry (2015), horror POV, video-game-style sequences.

Second-Person

Perspective

The camera or a character addresses you, the audience, directly — in film, this is the fourth-wall break: a character looks into the lens and speaks to us, making us a character in the scene.

Effect / purposeComplicity, comedy, intimacy or confrontation. It shatters the illusion on purpose.

Watch outOnce broken, the wall is hard to rebuild — use it as a consistent device, not a one-off gag, unless the gag is the point.

ExampleDeadpool, Fleabag (TV), Ferris Bueller's Day Off — direct address as narration and confession.

Third-Person

Perspective

The camera watches the story from outside the characters — the default of most cinema. Subdivided into omniscient and limited (next cards).

Effect / purposeFlexibility: we can follow anyone, see anything, and know more or less than any character.

ExampleAlmost all narrative film.

Omniscient

Perspective

Third-person with total knowledge: the camera can go anywhere, show any character, and reveal information no character has — bird's-eye and god-like views included.

Effect / purposeMastery, irony — we know the bomb is under the table — epic scope, fate.

ExampleHitchcock's "bomb under the table" suspense; omniscient narration in epics; overhead god's-eye shots.

Limited

Perspective

Third-person restricted to one character: the camera stays close to their experience and knowledge, even when it is not literally their POV. We see their face, follow them, learn when they learn.

Effect / purposeIdentification without losing the face; suspense through shared ignorance.

ExampleA thriller that follows one detective; a coming-of-age film that never leaves its protagonist's orbit.

Character POV vs Audience POV

Perspective

Character POV: what a character sees and knows (POV shot, eyeline match). Audience POV: what we see and know — which may be more, or less, than the character's.

Effect / purposeThe gap between the two is where suspense lives. Close the gap for empathy; widen it for irony or dread.

ExampleHorror: the audience sees the threat, the character does not (dramatic irony). Mystery: audience and detective discover together.

Breaking the Fourth Wall

Perspective

A character acknowledges the camera and audience — looks into the lens, speaks to us, comments on being in a film. The "fourth wall" is the imaginary wall between stage or screen and audience; breaking it violates the convention that actors pretend we are not there.

Effect / purposeMeta-comedy, narration, a character recruiting the audience as an ally — the mechanism of second-person address.

ExampleDeadpool; Fleabag; Frank Underwood's asides in House of Cards.

Voyeuristic / Observational

Perspective

The camera watches as if unseen — long lenses, hidden positions, long takes, no acknowledgement, subjects unaware or unposed. The audience becomes a voyeur: present, invisible, and slightly complicit.

Effect / purposeRealism, unease, intimacy without permission, documentary truth — and, deliberately, discomfort about watching.

Watch outIn real documentary work this raises ethics (consent, privacy) as well as aesthetics; in fiction it can make the audience feel guilty for enjoying a private moment — use that guilt on purpose, or avoid it.

ExampleRear Window (1954), voyeurism as theme; "fly on the wall" documentary; long-lens surveillance-style shots in thrillers.

Category 05 · Where things sit in the frame

Composition & Framing

Composition is where things sit in the frame and how depth is built. These principles apply at any shot size — and every one of them can be broken on purpose, once you know what the unbroken version says.

Composition lab · Place the figure, guide the eye

Same valley, seven arrangements

Pick an arrangement, then drag the figure yourself with the slider. Toggle the guide overlays to see the hidden geometry — thirds lines sit at 33%, phi lines at ~38% / 62%, and they are not the same grid. The verdict line tells you when an arrangement works — and when it traps the figure against the edge.

Rule of Thirds

How to build it
Watch out

Rule of Thirds

Composition

Divide the frame into a 3×3 grid. Place key elements — especially eyes, or the horizon — on the lines or at the four intersections ("power points").

Effect / purposeDynamic, natural-feeling balance; the eye has somewhere to travel. Horizon on the upper third makes the shot about the land; on the lower third, about the sky.

When to useThe default for portraits, landscapes and dialogue.

Break it forSymmetry, a centred icon, or a tiny figure in vast emptiness (negative space). Note: thirds is not the golden ratio — thirds sit at 33%, phi lines at ~38% / 62%.

Golden Ratio / Phi Grid

Composition

Proportions of ~1 : 1.618. A phi grid places lines at ~38% and ~62%; a golden spiral coils from a corner toward the focal point.

Effect / purposeA subtler, more "inevitable" harmony than thirds; the eye travels a curve rather than parking on a grid cell.

When to usePainterly portraits, landscapes where a path, tree or figure genuinely coils, designed interiors.

Watch outIt only works if masses in the frame actually sit on the curve — overlaying a spiral on a random frame is decoration, not composition.

ExampleThe painterly framing of Barry Lyndon; landscape spirals in The Tree of Life.

Leading Lines

Composition

Real or implied lines — roads, fences, rivers, corridors, a row of people, a gaze — that pull the eye toward the subject or through the frame.

Effect / purposeDepth, direction, inevitability.

When to useGuiding attention in a busy wide shot; making a corridor feel like a journey; pointing at a reveal.

Watch outLines that lead the eye out of the frame instead of to the subject.

Symmetry

Composition

Mirrored, centred composition.

Effect / purposeOrder, formality, ritual, artificiality, control — or, when broken by one element, a jarring wrongness.

When to useCentred, designed worlds; one-point-perspective corridors; ceremonial scenes. Break it with one off-centre element to signal disorder.

ExampleWes Anderson's centred worlds; Kubrick's one-point perspective corridors.

Depth of Field DoF

Composition

How much of the image, front to back, is in sharp focus — controlled by aperture, focal length and subject distance.

Shallow DoFWide aperture, low f-number, longer lens, close subject: the subject is sharp and the background melts into bokeh. Isolation, intimacy, dreaminess — "look only here".

Deep focusSmall aperture, wide lens, bright light: foreground, midground and background all sharp. The audience chooses where to look; geography and simultaneity matter.

ExampleCitizen Kane (1941) — a child playing outside the window while adults argue in the foreground, all sharp, in one shot.

Foreground / Midground / Background

Composition

Layering elements at three depths — a blurred branch in the foreground, the actor in the midground, a city in the background.

Effect / purposeThree-dimensionality, parallax when the camera moves, a sense of a world beyond the subject.

Watch outA shot with everything at one distance looks flat — "talking heads against a wall". Forgetting the foreground is one of the most common framing mistakes.

Negative Space

Composition

Empty or near-empty area around the subject.

Effect / purposeIsolation, loneliness, breathing room, importance — a tiny figure in a huge sky is the point — or calm before a shock.

When to useA lone character after a loss; a minimalist product shot; a horror frame where the empty dark half is where the threat could be.

Watch outNegative space without intent reads as an accident.

Headroom / Look Room / Nose Room

Composition

Headroom: the space above the head. Look room (nose room): the space in front of a subject's face, in the direction they are looking or moving.

Effect / purposeToo much headroom and the subject sinks; too little and it feels claustrophobic. A character looking screen-right needs space on the right, or they feel trapped against the edge. A useful guide for interviews and dialogue: roughly the eye-to-chin distance above the head.

Watch outClipping the top of the head is fine in an ECU (intentional cropping) but reads as a mistake in a medium shot. Headroom that changes randomly between coverage shots breaks a conversation.

Frame within a Frame

Composition

A doorway, window, arch, mirror, foliage or corridor creates a second frame around the subject.

Effect / purposeDepth, voyeurism — we are peeking — entrapment, or a character boxed in by their world.

ExampleCharacters seen through doorways in The Godfather and Parasite.

Silhouette

Composition

The subject rendered as a dark shape against a bright background, all detail removed.

Effect / purposeMystery, iconography, menace, universality — we project onto a shape.

When to useA figure on a horizon at sunset, a villain's entrance, a title image.

Watch outAn accidentally underexposed subject just looks like a lighting error.

Reflections & Mirrors

Composition

Mirrors, windows, water and polished surfaces show a second view of a subject or world.

Effect / purposeDuality, a hidden self, vanity, a character watching themselves — or a reveal: the reflection shows what the character cannot see.

When to useA character's double life; a thriller reveal in a mirror; a symmetrical reflection composition.

ExampleMirror shots in Black Swan (duality); Lady in the Lake, where the hero is visible only in mirrors.

Common mistakes — composition: centring everything by default; ignoring look room so a character stares into a wall of frame edge; no foreground layer, so the image is flat; a horizon cutting through a head; leading lines that lead the eye out of the frame.
Category 06 · The grammar that binds shots together

Advanced Terms & Topics

Staging, continuity, editing patterns, lenses, light and colour — the systems that make individual shots add up to scenes. Two hands-on labs teach the hardest ideas — where the camera is allowed to stand (the 180-degree rule) and how choices combine into meaning (the sentence builder) — and aspect ratio gets its own lab at the end of this category.

Continuity lab · Where is the camera allowed to stand?

The 180-degree rule, from above

A faces B. The dashed line between them is the axis of action. Cameras 1, 2 and 3 all stand on the same (south) side of it — cut between them and A always appears on the left looking right, B on the right looking left. Now try camera X, across the line, and watch the screen flip.

On set — view from above (click a camera)

On screen — what that camera sees

Shot-reverse-shot is built from positions like 2 and 3: over A's shoulder, then over B's, both from the same side of the line, with matching eyelines and shot sizes. Cross the line only on purpose — to disorient — and reset it with a neutral head-on or overhead shot, or by visibly moving a character across the frame. The same side-of-the-line discipline protects screen direction: a character walking screen-right keeps walking screen-right.

Mise-en-scène

Advanced

French: "placing on stage". Everything placed in front of the camera and how it is arranged — set, props, costume, make-up, lighting, actors' positions and movement, and composition.

Effect / purposeMise-en-scène is the image's meaning before a word is spoken: a cluttered room reads as chaos, an empty room as isolation, and who stands where shows who has power.

With the cameraA wide shot lets mise-en-scène speak; a close-up cuts it away. The long-take tradition (Bazin) trusts staging and camera movement over cutting.

Blocking & Staging

Advanced

The planned movement and positioning of actors and camera in a scene — who moves where, when, and what the camera does in response.

Effect / purposeGood blocking makes power visible: a character who advances owns the scene; one who retreats, or is framed behind furniture, is diminished.

PracticeBlock the scene for the master shot first, then design coverage around the blocking — not the other way round.

Continuity Editing

Advanced

The classical Hollywood system for cutting so that space, time and action feel seamless — the audience should notice the story, not the cuts. Also called invisible editing.

Its toolsThe 180-degree rule, the 30-degree rule, eyeline match, match on action, and shot-reverse-shot — each has its own card in this category.

180-Degree Rule / Axis of Action

Advanced

Draw an imaginary line — the axis of action — between two characters, or along a moving subject's direction. The camera must stay on one side of that line for the whole scene.

WhyCross the line and screen left/right flip: a character who was looking right now looks left, a car travelling right now travels left — and the audience is momentarily lost.

Breaking itDeliberately, only to disorient (a fight, a breakdown, a dream) — and ideally with a neutral shot, head-on or overhead, or a character crossing the frame, to "reset" the line.

30-Degree Rule

Advanced

Between two consecutive shots of the same subject, move the camera at least 30° — and/or change shot size significantly.

WhyA smaller change looks like a jump: the subject appears to "jump" in place rather than being seen from a new angle.

Breaking itViolating the rule creates a jump cut — which is a choice, not an accident, when done on purpose.

Shot-Reverse-Shot

Advanced

The dialogue pattern: a shot of A (often OTS), then a reverse shot of B from the other end of the axis, then back to A, and so on.

Effect / purposeA conversation feels natural, like turning your head between speakers. Eyelines and shot sizes should match across the pair.

ExampleVirtually every two-person dialogue scene ever shot.

Cross-Cutting / Parallel Editing

Advanced

Cutting back and forth between two or more actions in different places, presented as simultaneous.

Effect / purposeSuspense — "will they arrive in time?" — thematic comparison, or a race against the clock.

ExampleA rescue racing to a victim, intercut with the victim in danger; the baptism and murders intercut in The Godfather.

Match Cut

Advanced

A cut that links two shots by visual similarity — same shape, composition, movement or colour — across a change of time, place or subject.

Effect / purposeA poetic or conceptual link: A is B, or A becomes B.

ExampleThe bone thrown into the air cutting to a space station in 2001: A Space Odyssey; a door closing in one era cutting to a door opening in another.

Jump Cut

Advanced

A cut between two very similar shots of the same subject, with a piece of time (or a small camera move) missing, so the subject visibly "jumps".

Effect / purposeUrgency, disorientation, comedy, the passage of time, a character's fractured state. An error in classical continuity; a style in New Wave and modern editing.

ExampleGodard's Breathless (1960); modern vlog editing; a character's frantic montage.

Long Take / One-Shot

Advanced

A shot of extended duration with no (visible) cuts — a whole scene, or in extreme cases a whole film. Also called a plan-séquence.

Effect / purposeImmersion, real time, tension — no escape via a cut — and virtuosity.

Watch outA long take that shows off technique instead of story becomes a demo reel; the move must be motivated by what the character experiences.

ExampleRussian Ark (2002), a single 96-minute Steadicam shot; Birdman (2014) and 1917 (2019), edited to appear continuous via hidden cuts; the car ambush and war-zone takes in Children of Men (2006).

Montage

Advanced

A series of short shots cut together to condense time and space, or to create a single idea from juxtaposition.

Two traditionsHollywood montage compresses time — a training sequence, a journey, a relationship growing. Soviet / Eisensteinian montage creates meaning by collision: shot A + shot B = a third idea neither contains alone (the Kuleshov effect: the same neutral face reads as hunger, grief or desire depending on the shot it is cut against).

ExampleThe training montage in Rocky; the Odessa Steps in Battleship Potemkin (1925).

Lens Choice & Focal Length

Advanced

Focal length changes not just how much you see, but how space feels. A dolly-in on a wide lens and a zoom-in on a telephoto can frame the same face and feel completely different.

Wide (≤35mm; ultra-wide 12–24mm)Wide field of view, exaggerated perspective — near things loom, far things shrink, space feels deep; distortion at the edges. Environments, interiors, unease, a character dwarfed by a room.

Normal (35–50mm)Closest to human vision, least distortion; the versatile workhorse.

Medium telephoto (50–85mm)Flattering for faces, moderate compression, clean background separation; the classic portrait and dialogue lens.

Telephoto (85–200mm+)Narrow field of view and compression: the background appears pulled close, space flattens, a distant crowd looks dense, a road looks stacked. Surveillance and voyeurism, isolating a subject, sport. Overused in action, it can make geography unreadable.

Aperture & Exposure

Advanced

Aperture is the size of the lens opening — f-stop on stills lenses, T-stop on cinema lenses (which measures actual light transmission). Exposure balances aperture + shutter speed + ISO.

The ruleLower f-number (f/1.8, T1.3) = wider opening = more light + shallower depth of field. Higher f-number (f/16) = smaller opening = less light + deeper focus.

Creative useA fast, wide aperture at night for bokeh and subject separation; a stopped-down aperture in bright daylight for deep-focus landscapes.

Watch outAt T1.3 on a long lens, depth of field can be razor-thin — a subject leaning forward can fall out of focus mid-line.

Colour Palette & Colour Theory

Advanced

Colour is story, not decoration. Hue, saturation and contrast are set on set — production design, costume, light colour — and refined in grading.

Warm vs coolWarm (reds, oranges, golds; low Kelvin) = comfort, intimacy, nostalgia, desire — pushed far, danger and heat. Cool (blues, greens, greys; high Kelvin) = distance, sadness, sterility, unease, night.

Key pairingsComplementary pairs — teal/orange is the famous blockbuster pairing — create contrast: warm skin against a cool world. Monochromatic palettes give unity, bleakness or sophistication. Desaturated reads bleak, historical, exhausted; saturated reads vital, fantastic, comic.

ArcA palette should change with the character: a world that starts grey and gains colour as a character awakens is a classic arc.

ExampleDesaturated Kansas to saturated Oz in The Wizard of Oz; the colour-coded chapters of Moonlight.

High-Key & Low-Key Lighting

Advanced

High-key: bright, even, soft light, low contrast, few deep shadows. Low-key: little fill light, high contrast, large areas of darkness, pools of light.

FeelHigh-key feels open, cheerful, safe, honest — comedy, musicals, romance, daytime TV (Pretty Woman, 1990). Low-key feels moody, tense, secretive, dangerous — noir, horror, thriller (The Maltese Falcon, 1941; M, 1931).

With the cameraLighting angle and camera angle interact: a low angle + low key + rim light makes a looming villain; the same angle in high key makes a hero.

Chiaroscuro

Advanced

Italian: "light–dark". Strong, sculptural contrast between light and shadow, borrowed from Renaissance painting.

Effect / purposeDrama and moral ambiguity — a face half in light, half in dark is a divided character.

ExampleNosferatu (1922), The Third Man (1949), and film noir generally.

Motivated & Practical Lighting

Advanced

Motivated lighting appears to come from a source visible or plausible in the scene — a window, a lamp, a TV, moonlight — even if the real fixture is off-camera. Practicals are lamps, candles and neon signs that are in the frame and sometimes actually light it.

Effect / purposeMotivated light feels believable and grounded. Its opposite, unmotivated or stylised light, is used for effect — and should be a deliberate choice.

Key / fill / backThe three-point base: the key is the main light (direction plus character), the fill softens shadows, and the back or rim light separates the subject from the background with an edge of light.

ExampleBlade Runner 2049 (2017) mixes practicals with motivated light.

Camera Height vs Angle

Advanced

Height is where the camera sits — on the ground, at knee, hip, shoulder or eye level, on a crane. Angle is where it points — up, down, level, rolled. They are independent.

Why it mattersYou can be at knee height pointing level (a child's eye view, neutral), at eye height pointing down (looking down at a seated person), or at ground level pointing up (worm's-eye).

Watch outConfusing the two is the most common beginner error: "low angle" describes the tilt up, not merely a low camera.

Eye-Line Match

Advanced

When a character looks off-screen, the next shot shows what they are looking at, from a position that matches their gaze direction and height — and eyeline height stays consistent across a shot-reverse-shot pair.

WhyIt convinces the audience the two shots share a space. Break it, and characters appear to look past each other.

Screen Direction

Advanced

The consistent left/right (and toward/away) direction of movement and gaze across cuts.

WhyA character walking screen-right must keep walking screen-right in the next shot, unless they have visibly turned. Screen direction is what the 180-degree rule protects.

Aspect Ratio

Advanced

The width : height of the frame. It shapes composition before a single shot is chosen. Try them all in the lab below this category.

4:3 (1.33:1)Classic TV and early cinema: boxy, intimate, vertical-friendly, nostalgic. Used today for period or claustrophobic films — The Lighthouse, A Ghost Story; The Grand Budapest Hotel uses it for its 1930s sequences.

16:9 (1.78:1)HDTV and YouTube standard; a balanced, natural wide frame; the default for TV and online video.

1.85:1One of the two standard US cinema formats ("flat"); slightly wider than 16:9.

2.39:1 (Scope)The widest standard cinema format: epic, landscape, ensemble, horizontal movement; letterboxed on a 16:9 screen. Anamorphic lenses squeeze the wide image onto the sensor and unsqueeze it in projection, giving oval bokeh and horizontal flares.

9:16 (vertical)Phone-first short form — see the Director's Guide.

ChoosingA wider ratio favours landscapes, groups and lateral movement; a narrower ratio favours faces, verticality and intimacy. Changing ratio within a film can signal a change of era, scale or reality — use it sparingly.

Combination lab · Size + angle + movement = meaning

Build a shot sentence

Directors rarely choose one thing at a time — they choose a combination, and the combination is a sentence the audience reads instantly. Pick a size, an angle and a movement (or tap a preset) and read what your shot says. Then change just one choice and watch the sentence change.

1 · Shot size — how much of her?

2 · Angle — from where?

3 · Movement — how does the camera behave?

Presets — the three sentences from the Director's Guide

Aspect ratio lab

Same image, five frames

The set illustration from the top of this guide, reframed at each standard ratio. Watch what each frame keeps — and what it throws away.

16:9 · 1.78:1

16:9 — the broadcast standard

Category 07 · Making the impossible — and bending time

Special Effects

Effects divide by where they happen: practical effects are built and filmed for real on set; visual effects (VFX) are created or altered in post-production, usually with computers; in-camera effects are tricks of lens, set and perspective that fool the camera itself. A fourth family changes time and space inside the shot — and therefore changes how the shot is read.

Practical Effects SFX

Effects

Effects created physically, in front of the camera, on the day: explosions, rain and wind machines, prosthetic make-up, animatronics, puppets, squibs, breakaway props, real stunt work.

How it readsReal light on real matter. Actors react to something that is actually there, debris obeys real physics, and the effect ages well because it was photographed, not rendered.

When to useCreature and make-up effects, weather, destruction the cast must interact with, and any effect where physical contact sells the shot.

Watch outOne take can destroy the set — resets are slow and expensive — and safety governs everything: the effect must be designed around the people near it.

ExampleThe animatronic and prosthetic creatures of The Thing (1982); the real vehicle stunts and explosions of Mad Max: Fury Road (2015).

Visual Effects / CGI VFX

Effects

Imagery created or altered in post-production: computer-generated characters, creatures and environments, compositing (layering separately shot elements), digital set extensions, wire removal, de-ageing.

How it readsAnything is possible — which is the risk. CGI that ignores the scene's lighting, lens and camera movement looks pasted on; CGI built from the photographed plate, with matching grain, focus and camera shake, disappears.

When to useThe impossible, the unsafe and the extinct: fantasy creatures, destroyed cities, historical worlds, shots no camera could survive.

Watch outWeightlessness — digital objects and cameras with no mass or inertia feel unreal (the same trap as CG camera moves). Most modern "practical" films are in fact hybrids: practical plates extended and cleaned up with VFX.

ExampleThe fully digital world of Avatar (2009); the set extensions and crowd multiplication of large-scale epics and superhero films.

In-Camera Effects

Effects

Tricks achieved in the camera or on the set at the moment of shooting, with no post-production: double exposure, mirrors, glass (matte) shots painted on glass between camera and set, rear projection behind the actors, split-focus diopters.

How it readsBecause the trick is photographed in one pass, light, grain and focus agree across the whole frame — the oldest effects often feel the most solid.

When to useLow budgets, stylised or period looks, and any effect that must play in a single unbroken take.

Watch outThe camera is usually locked off and the actors' movement is limited — one wrong step breaks the alignment.

ExampleGlass matte paintings extending castles and cities in classic Hollywood; the mirror and split-diopter shots of Brian De Palma's films.

Miniatures & Forced Perspective

Effects

Two classic in-camera scale tricks. Miniatures: small-scale models filmed (often in slow motion, so gravity looks right at scale) as stand-ins for full-size buildings, ships and cities. Forced perspective: objects placed at calculated distances so a near small thing and a far large thing read as the same scale.

How it readsScale and depth are created by geometry, not computation — real light, real focus fall-off, real atmosphere.

When to useMonumental sets on a fraction of the budget; size differences between characters sharing one frame.

Watch outBoth demand a locked or carefully limited camera, and depth of field must cover the near and far elements at once.

ExampleThe miniature spacecraft of 2001: A Space Odyssey and the original Star Wars; forced perspective making hobbits small beside Gandalf in The Lord of the Rings.

Dolly Zoom (Vertigo Effect)

Effects

The camera dollies in one direction while the zoom moves in the opposite direction, at matched rates. The subject stays the same size while the background stretches or squeezes behind them.

How it readsThe world warps around a fixed face: vertigo, dread, a sudden realisation, the ground dropping out of a moment. Space itself seems to change its mind.

When to useSparingly, at a story peak: a character understands something terrible, or the world tilts for them.

Watch outIt is one of the most recognisable effects in cinema — used casually, it reads as a quotation rather than a feeling.

ExampleVertigo (1958), Scottie looking down the stairwell; Jaws (1975), Brody's realisation on the beach; Frodo sensing the Nazgûl in The Fellowship of the Ring.

Slow Motion

Effects

Shoot at a higher frame rate than playback (overcranking): film at 48, 96 or 240 frames per second, play back at 24, and time stretches.

How it readsGravity, impact and emotion are magnified; the audience is given time to feel an instant. Violence becomes balletic or horrifying; a mundane gesture becomes monumental.

When to useImpacts, falls, realisations, heroic or terrible instants the story wants to hold open.

Watch outSlow motion flatters almost anything, so overuse drains it — and sound design must be rebuilt, since real sound no longer matches.

ExampleThe balletic gunfights of The Wild Bunch (1969) and John Woo's films; the stylised battles of 300 (2006).

Time-Lapse

Effects

The opposite of slow motion: frames are captured at long intervals (or the camera is undercranked) and played at normal speed, so slow change becomes fast.

How it readsTime becomes visible: clouds pour, crowds flow like water, cities breathe, plants and decay move like animals. Human presence shrinks to a pattern.

When to usePassage of time, natural processes, a city or landscape as a living system, transitions between eras.

Watch outFlicker from changing light, and subjects that leave the frame between frames — plan the interval for the speed of the process, not the clock.

ExampleThe city and nature sequences of Koyaanisqatsi (1982).

Speed Ramping

Effects

The playback speed changes within a single shot — normal speed flows into slow motion and back, usually across an impact or a key gesture.

How it readsThe shot breathes: real time for the approach, stretched time for the moment that matters, real time for the consequence. Attention is steered inside the shot without a cut.

When to useAction beats, impacts, a fighter reading an opponent, sport.

Watch outRamping on every beat turns a signature into a tic; the ramp must land on the story's beat, not just the loudest frame.

ExampleThe fights of 300 (2006) and Sherlock Holmes (2009).

Split-Screen

Effects

Two or more separate images shown at once inside one frame, divided by a visible border or a seamless join.

How it readsSimultaneity and comparison: two places at the same moment, a caller and the called, cause beside effect, expectation beside reality. The audience edits the relationship themselves.

When to usePhone calls, parallel action too interdependent for cross-cutting, contrasting two versions of one moment.

Watch outAttention splits too — keep one panel dominant, or the audience reads neither.

ExampleThe phone scenes of Pillow Talk (1959); Brian De Palma's set pieces; the real-time panels of TV's 24.

Bullet Time

Effects

An array of still cameras fires in sequence (or all at once) around a subject; the frames are interpolated into a shot where time nearly stops while the viewpoint keeps moving.

How it readsTime and viewpoint are uncoupled: the moment freezes, but we can still walk around it. Superhuman perception made visible.

When to useA character whose awareness outruns the world — dodging, perceiving, deciding inside an instant.

Watch outIt became so identified with one film that it now reads as homage; the rig and interpolation are also unforgiving of moving backgrounds.

ExampleNeo dodging bullets on the rooftop in The Matrix (1999).

Effects change how a shot is read, not just what it shows

A dolly zoom keeps the face and warps the world, so we read psychology. Slow motion stretches an instant, so we read weight. Time-lapse compresses hours, so we read systems, not people. Split-screen divides the frame, so we read relationships. Choose the effect for the reading you want — the spectacle is the side effect.

Putting it together

The Practical Director's Guide

How shot choice creates feeling — tension, intimacy, power, isolation, comedy — and how to pick the combination on purpose. (This section is a synthesis: it stays visible under every filter.)

Choose by the feeling you want

FeelingGo to firstAvoid / be careful with
Intimacy / love / confessionMCU/CU, eye-level, slow push-in or static, shallow DoF, warm soft lightWide shots (distance), Dutch angles (unease), handheld shake (anxiety)
Power / dominanceLow angle, wide lens, pedestal or crane up, high-contrast light, subject advancing to cameraHigh angle, soft high-key light, a subject small in a wide frame
Vulnerability / powerlessnessHigh angle, wide shot, negative space, cool low-key light, slow pull-backLow angle, tight heroic framing
Tension / dreadSlow push-in, locked-off frame, shallow focus, low-key / chiaroscuro, cross-cutting, a long take with no releaseFast cutting that releases tension too early; a cheerful high-key look
Isolation / lonelinessEWS, negative space, static or pull-back camera, desaturated / cool palette, a character with no look roomTwo-shots, warm close coverage
ComedyObjective locked-off wide (deadpan), snap zoom or whip pan as punctuation, a grand move for a trivial subjectShaky handheld (reads as panic, not funny), Dutch angles (reads as unease)
Wonder / scaleEWS, crane or drone rise, deep focus, slow revealTight close-ups that hide the world
Chaos / urgencyHandheld, whip pans, jump cuts, fast cross-cutting, telephoto compression in a crowdSmooth Steadicam (too calm), long static takes

Choose by the job you need to do

JobBest tools
Orient the audienceEstablishing wide, master shot, crane or drone rise
Follow a conversationMaster → OTS shot-reverse-shot → singles (MCU/CU), eyeline match, 180-degree rule
Follow a journeyTracking / follow shot, Steadicam, an arc for a turning point
Reveal a secretRack focus, a reveal move (pan / dolly / crane past foreground), match cut, insert
Compress timeMontage, jump cuts, cross-cutting, time-lapse
Build a set-pieceLong take with Steadicam or crane, then coverage for rhythm in the edit

Same subject, three sentences

Combining angle + movement + size changes the meaning, not just the look:

CU + eye-level + static

"Listen to what she feels."

Intimacy, honesty.
CU + low angle + slow push-in

"She is becoming dangerous."

The same face, now a threat — power.
EWS + high angle + slow pull-back

"She is alone in a world that does not care."

The same person, now insignificant — isolation.

Change one variable and the sentence changes: a push-in says "we are drawn in"; a pull-back says "we are shut out". A low angle says "look up to them"; a high angle says "look down on them". A handheld romantic walk says "this is real and unstable"; a Steadicam version says "this is a dream". Directing is choosing which sentence to write, then making every department — lens, light, colour, blocking, edit — write the same sentence.

On-set checklist: (1) What must the audience feel in this shot? (2) What must they know — geography, clue, relationship? (3) Which single move, size and angle delivers both? (4) What is the simplest version of that shot? Shoot the simple version first — usually the master — then the expressive version. You can always cut back to simple; you cannot invent coverage you never shot.

Mistakes that cross every category

  • Moving the camera without a story reason; using every technique in one scene ("showreel directing").
  • Breaking the 180° or 30° rule by accident — if you break a rule, break it loudly and on purpose.
  • Inconsistent eyelines, headroom or look room between coverage shots, so a conversation feels like two different rooms.
  • A close-up for geography, a wide shot for an emotion, a Dutch angle for a neutral scene.
  • Forgetting the foreground: flat, single-plane framing with no depth layering.
  • Overusing zoom when a dolly would immerse; overusing handheld when the scene needs calm.

Live-action vs animation

The language is the same; the constraints are opposite. Live-action records a real world with a real camera: you are limited by locations, light, weather, actor stamina and physics, but you gain real texture, real accidents and real human micro-expression — so camera choices are planned around what is physically possible on the day, and coverage protects the edit.

Animation (2D, 3D/CG, stop-motion) uses a virtual camera: in principle any angle, lens, move or world is possible, including impossible moves — through a keyhole, a 360° orbit around a frozen moment. The danger is the opposite of live-action: perfection. CG cameras that pivot with no weight, inertia or imperfection feel weightless and unreal, so good animation cinematography imitates real rigs — Steadicam-style movement at character scale, keyframed weight and inertia, lens-accurate depth of field, motivated lighting. In 2D, depth is faked with multiplane layering: foreground, midground and background planes moving at different speeds. Almost everything can be revised without a reshoot, which makes disciplined previsualisation (storyboards, previz) essential, or choices drift endlessly.

Rule for both: if a move would be impossible or pointless with a real camera, ask whether its impossibility is the point — a dream, a superpower, a stylised world. If not, ground it.

Horizontal cinema vs vertical short-form (9:16)

Horizontal (16:9, 1.85:1, 2.39:1) rewards width: two-shots, ensembles, landscapes, lateral movement (tracking, pans) and layered depth across the frame — the grammar of cinema and TV, for a seated, captive audience where geography matters.

Vertical (9:16) rewards height and proximity: faces become landscapes, full-body movement runs floor-to-ceiling, movement goes toward and away from the audience (down the Z-axis) rather than across the frame, and the story is carried by one decisive gesture or motion per shot. Two-shots and wide establishing shots are hard; close-ups, singles and stacked foreground/subject/background layers work best. Keep critical action and text out of platform UI safe zones (on TikTok, the bottom ~20% and right ~10–15% are commonly covered), hook in the first 1–2 seconds, and design for a distracted, scrolling viewer — one emotional event per clip.

Shoot native; don't just crop. Cropping a 4K 16:9 frame to 9:16 keeps only about the centre third (~1215×2160) and throws away any subject near the edges. If you need both formats, shoot 4K+ (or open-gate, using the full sensor) with subjects centred and framing looser than usual — or shoot natively vertical when vertical is the primary deliverable.

What transfers unchanged: shot sizes, angles, eyelines, the 180-degree rule, and look room — now vertical look room too: space above a moving head, space in the direction of travel. And the core rule: move for a reason, and let size + angle + movement write one sentence at a time.

  • Vertical & animation broadcastprome.com — mastering the 9:16 frame · toneproduction.net — vertical framing · inorain.com — vertical filmmaking · expandedcinematography.com — The Lego Movie

Open points, stated plainly: sources differ slightly on the medium close-up (chest-up vs waist-up) and on whether the medium shot is waist-up or knees-up; this guide gives the most common convention and flags the variation. Statistics about audience response in some secondary sources were not relied on, as they were not corroborated by a second independent source.
